title: Data Scientist: is the pattern real, and how big is it?
intro: A scientist separates real effects from luck. It starts with a clear business question and the right data, then hypotheses, careful tests with several models, honest effect sizes, and finally telling the story. Say 'we can't tell yet' when that is true.
outcome: A short write-up: question, test, result with effect size and uncertainty, limits, and a recommendation.

steps.title: Clarify the business question
steps.what: The first and most important step: it decides how the whole project goes.
how: Ask what decision the answer will change, and who will make it.
Write the question in one sentence a non-expert would understand (Analysis Lab, Data foundations, DS methodology: the 10-stage project note).
Note what a good answer looks like and the deadline.
steps.done_when: A one-sentence question and the decision it serves are written down (a Data plan note works).
mistakes: Starting with the data instead of the question.
A question too broad to answer.
steps.ask: Help me turn a vague worry about my business into a testable question.

steps.title: Decide what data you need and where it comes from
steps.what: Structured and unstructured data, from many sources, can be analyzed.
how: List the information the question needs and possible sources (your files, public data, surveys, logs, text).
Check privacy and licence before using it.
Record it in a Data plan note and import it in My data.
steps.done_when: Each needed field has a named source, and you know what is missing.
mistakes: Using whatever data is nearby.
Ignoring text or notes that hold the reason.
steps.ask: What data would I need to answer my question, and where could I get it?

steps.title: Write a testable hypothesis
steps.what: A claim you can be wrong about.
how: State the null (no difference) and the alternative.
Choose the outcome measure and the groups before looking.
Write the smallest difference that would matter to the business.
steps.done_when: H0, H1, the measure and the 'matters' threshold are written down.
mistakes: Choosing the question after seeing the result.
No minimum meaningful effect.
steps.ask: Help me write a null and alternative hypothesis for weekend versus weekday revenue.

steps.title: Check the data is suitable
steps.what: A test needs enough observations in each group.
how: Look at the readiness strip on this page: weekend and weekday day counts.
Check data quality on the Data quality page.
If a group has under ~5 days, collect more data instead of testing.
steps.done_when: Both groups have enough days and the quality checks pass.
mistakes: Testing 2 days against 20.
Ignoring duplicates.
steps.ask: Is my data big enough for a weekend versus weekday test?

steps.title: Prepare the data (the longest step)
steps.what: Preparation typically takes 70 to 90 percent of a project; skipping it sends you back to the drawing board.
how: Inspect the table, then fix missing values, duplicates, wrong types and placeholder codes such as 999 (Analysis Lab, Data foundations, Data cleaning).
Add columns that carry business knowledge: ratios, month, size groups, yes/no flags, and a yes/no outcome such as returns within 30 days.
Roll transactions up to one row per customer or account (One row per entity), then log what you did.
steps.done_when: The table has one row per entity, a clearly defined outcome, no leftover issues on re-inspection, and every change is in the Wrangling log.
mistakes: Using the raw transactions as if each row were a separate customer.
A column built from the outcome itself, which leaks the answer.
steps.ask: Inspect my table and tell me what to fix and which columns to add before modeling.

steps.title: Understand the tables you query
steps.what: Know the keys, the links and what one row means before you join anything.
how: Open Analysis Lab > Data foundations > Relational design.
Analyze the table you are about to use: its candidate keys tell you what one row is, and its rules show where values repeat.
Check which columns link to other tables before you join, so you don't multiply rows.
steps.done_when: You can say what one row of each table means and which column joins it to the next.
mistakes: Joining on a column that isn't unique and counting twice.
Assuming a rule holds because it held in a few rows.
steps.ask: What is one row in this table, and what should I join it on?

steps.title: Use the SQL and pandas cookbook
steps.what: Look up a cleaning recipe, practise interview-style SQL, or find the pandas line for a job.
how: Open Analysis Lab > Data foundations > SQL & pandas cookbook.
Run a recipe on the sample to see before and after, then apply the same idea to your own table with the Data cleaning tab (it makes a copy and logs each step).
Work through the 50 SQL interview questions: try your own answer in SQL Lab first, then compare.
steps.done_when: You can clean a column in SQL and say which rows an UPDATE or DELETE would change before running it.
mistakes: Running UPDATE or DELETE on the only copy of the data.
Copying MySQL syntax (IFNULL, STR_TO_DATE, LOCATE) into DuckDB.
Forgetting the 'g' flag in regexp_replace, which cleans only the first match.
steps.ask: Which cleaning recipe fits my messy column, and how do I check it first?

steps.title: Describe before you test
steps.what: Look at the distributions and relationships first.
how: Read the correlations and segments panels on the workbench.
Open notebook 11 for hands-on examples.
Look for outliers that could drive the result.
steps.done_when: You can describe each group's centre and spread in a sentence.
mistakes: Jumping to a test with an outlier unexamined.
Reading correlation as cause.
steps.ask: Explain the correlations panel in plain words.

steps.title: Run the test and read it properly
steps.what: The Welch t-test compares two group means without assuming equal spread.
how: Read the weekend test panel: both means, the difference, the p-value, and the confidence interval.
A small p-value says 'unlikely to be luck', not 'important'.
Compare the effect size to your 'matters' threshold from step 1.
steps.done_when: You can state the difference in dollars and its interval.
mistakes: Treating p < 0.05 as proof.
Reporting only the p-value.
steps.ask: Interpret my weekend test result: is it real and does it matter?

steps.title: Segment and cluster
how: Read the entity segments panel.
Try several models on the same question (Analysis Lab: Clusters, Outliers, Decision tree, Bought together) and see which patterns, archetypes and outliers repeat.
Name each cluster in business terms.
steps.done_when: Each segment has a name and one action, and you know which findings more than one method agrees on.
mistakes: Too many clusters to explain.
Clusters that only restate size.
steps.ask: Describe the segments in my data and what to do about each.

steps.title: Model: descriptive or predictive, trained on known outcomes
steps.what: Modeling is where you taste the sauce: does it need more seasoning?
how: Decide the type: a descriptive model finds patterns (people who do this prefer that: Clusters, Associations); a predictive model gives a yes/no or a number (Decision tree, ML Lab).
For a predictive model use a training set of past records whose outcomes are known, and hold some back to test on.
Try more than one algorithm, always against a baseline, and drop variables that add nothing.
steps.done_when: You compared at least two algorithms to a baseline on held-back data and can name the variables that matter.
mistakes: Judging a model on the rows it trained on.
Keeping every variable because it was available.
steps.ask: Which model type fits my question, and how should I train and compare them?

steps.title: Evaluate: does the model answer the original question?
steps.what: Evaluation runs alongside modeling and happens before anything is put to use.
how: Diagnostic phase: read accuracy against the baseline on held-back rows, then sensitivity and specificity for the outcome you care about (Analysis Lab, Decision tree).
Tune the relative cost of a miss (1, 2, 4, 9 to 1) and read the ROC curve: the best setting sits furthest above the chance line for the mix of hits and false alarms you can afford.
Then check significance (could this beat the baseline by luck?) and go back to the original question: if the model doesn't answer it, adjust the data or the model.
steps.done_when: You can say which setting you chose and why, in terms of the cost of a miss versus a false alarm, and whether the result is more than luck.
mistakes: Picking the model with the best overall accuracy when a miss is expensive.
Declaring victory without checking the original question.
steps.ask: Which cost setting should I choose, and does my model answer the business question?

steps.title: Deploy: get it used, start small, keep watching
steps.what: A good answer only matters once the people who must act on it are using it.
how: Write a Deployment plan: the owner, each stakeholder's need, how users will receive the answer (report, dashboard, scheduled refresh) and how fresh data reaches it.
Roll out to a small pilot first, train the users on reading the result and what action to take, then widen.
Decide what you will track after launch (the business number, drift in incoming data) and how feedback returns to you. The ML Lab's model registry can score new rows and check drift.
steps.done_when: A pilot group, a training plan, a success measure and a feedback route are written down.
mistakes: Handing over a model with no explanation of what to do with it.
Launching to everyone with no way to see it going wrong.
steps.ask: Draft a deployment plan for my model: pilot, training and monitoring.

steps.title: Feedback: measure the impact, refine, redeploy
steps.what: The more you learn the more you want to know: the methodology is a loop, not a line.
how: Name who owns the review and what business number you will compare.

Compare before and after the launch date (Data cleaning, Add a column, Before/after launch, then Compare groups). Where a control group isn't possible or fair, before and after is the honest alternative; say what else changed in that period.
Record the review in a Feedback note, list refinements (data you deferred, variables to redefine, actions to adjust), redeploy, and keep the loop going for the life of the solution.
steps.done_when: A dated review with a before/after number, a verdict and a list of refinements is saved.
mistakes: Crediting the model for a change that had another cause.
Never going back to refine.
steps.ask: How do I measure whether my model changed the outcome without a control group?

steps.title: Challenge your own conclusion
steps.what: Look for what else could explain the result.
how: List confounders (e.g. weekends have different entities).
Check the effect holds within segments.
Say what an experiment would need to prove cause.
steps.done_when: You listed at least two alternative explanations.
mistakes: Claiming cause from observational data.
Not saying what you didn't test.
steps.ask: What confounders could explain my weekend result?

steps.title: Write it up
steps.what: Make it usable by someone who skips the maths.
how: Lead with the answer in business terms, as a storyteller: situation, what the data revealed, what to do.
Give the effect size with its interval and one clear chart per point.
State limits and a next step.
steps.done_when: A non-technical reader could repeat your conclusion correctly and knows the recommended action.
mistakes: Jargon without a plain sentence beside it.
steps.ask: Draft the conclusion paragraph of my analysis.

steps.title: Compare forecasting methods and check what shape your data has
steps.what: BI work is mostly a handful of repeatable calculations. Practise each with the answer shown, so you can spot a wrong one in a real report.
how: Open the BI toolkit on this page. In the DAX lab run the three starter measures grouped by Country and say why 'USA Sales' repeats on every row (CALCULATE replaces the filter on that column).
In Forecast methods press Use infographic sample and compare the methods: say why a 3-point moving average loses to a trend method on a steadily rising series.
In Variance enter your own budget and actual lines; for each flag say whether it is favourable (revenue above budget is good, a cost above budget is not).
Run the scenario model and name the one driver with the biggest swing before you argue about the others.
Paste a sample invoice and bank statement into the Document reader; break one total on purpose and watch the check fail.
steps.done_when: You can explain one measure, one forecast ranking and one variance in plain words, with the arithmetic.
mistakes: Treating a method's good fit on past data as a promise about the future.
Reading a YTD or same-period-last-year figure from a function name without knowing the date table behind it.
Posting OCR output to a ledger without running the totals check.
steps.ask: Which forecasting method wins on my series, and is the gap big enough to matter?
